title: Why we fall for fake news
title_es: Por qué caemos en las noticias falsas

questions.q: What did the MIT researchers conclude?
options: False news spread further and faster than true news
Bots shared most of the false news
True news spread more widely than false news did
Twitter removed most false stories quickly
questions.answer: False news spread further and faster than true news
questions.why: Dice: false news spread further, faster and more widely than true news.

questions.q: According to the study, automated accounts were the main reason false news spread.
questions.why: Los principales culpables eran usuarios humanos comunes.

questions.q: Why does novelty help false stories spread?
options: Surprise grabs our attention
New stories are usually true
Novel stories are shorter to read
Bots prefer to share new stories
Accepting information that supports our existing beliefs
Checking every source very carefully
Trusting experts more than the opinions of our own friends
Rejecting news that sounds surprising
questions.answer: Accepting information that supports our existing beliefs

options: Familiarity can be mistaken for truth
It makes stories shorter each time
It makes readers bored and angry
It reduces the emotions we feel
questions.answer: Familiarity can be mistaken for truth
questions.why: Dice: familiarity can easily be mistaken for truth.

questions.q: Which question is NOT suggested before sharing a story?
options: How many likes does it have?
Who published it?
Do other reliable sources report it?
Is the photo recent?
questions.answer: How many likes does it have?
questions.why: No aparece entre las preguntas sugeridas.

questions.q: What effect did a short reminder about accuracy have?
options: People became less likely to share false headlines
People stopped using social media completely for a while
It made no real difference at all
People shared more news than before
questions.answer: People became less likely to share false headlines
questions.why: Dice: makes people noticeably less likely to share false headlines.

questions.q: What does the final sentence suggest?
options: Human nature is what makes misinformation spread
Technology alone is to blame for the problem
Algorithms will soon solve the problem
Misinformation is mostly harmless
questions.answer: Human nature is what makes misinformation spread
questions.why: Dice: it is our curiosity, our emotions… that give it wings.

questions.q: Find a word in paragraph 2 meaning 'a strong feeling of anger and shock': fear, disgust or ___.

task: Escribe 120–150 palabras: ¿alguna vez creíste o compartiste una noticia falsa? ¿Qué consejos darías para evitarlo?
paragraphs: A few years ago, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology analysed thousands of stories shared on Twitter over more than a decade. Their conclusion was striking: false news spread further, faster and more widely than true news. False stories were around seventy per cent more likely to be shared, and the main culprits were not automated accounts, or "bots", but ordinary human users.

Why should this be the case? One explanation is novelty. False stories are often surprising, and surprise grabs our attention. They also tend to provoke strong emotions such as fear, disgust or outrage, which make us want to react and share immediately, before we have stopped to think.

Another factor is what psychologists call confirmation bias: our tendency to accept information that supports what we already believe and to reject information that challenges it. If a headline confirms our view of a politician we dislike, we are less likely to question it. Repetition plays a part too. The more often we see a claim, the more familiar it feels, and familiarity can easily be mistaken for truth.

The good news is that some simple habits can reduce our vulnerability. Before sharing a story, it helps to pause and ask a few questions. Who published it? Is the same information reported by other reliable sources? Does the headline match the content of the article, or is it designed to make me click? Is the photo recent, or has it been taken out of context? Researchers have found that even a short reminder to think about accuracy makes people noticeably less likely to share false headlines.

Ultimately, misinformation is not only a technological problem but a human one. Algorithms may amplify it, but it is our curiosity, our emotions and our desire to belong to a group that give it wings.
